1.1.misconception: A figure that looks equal is equal. Surface it: students guess before measuring, then record guess vs. measured.

1.2.misconception: Enough examples prove a rule. Surface it: have them predict 6-point regions as 32 before counting 31.

1.3.misconception: Lines are segments with ends. Surface it: ask how many points a line has; anyone saying 'two' has the misconception.

1.4.misconception: Angle size depends on ray length. Surface it: show the same angle with long and short rays and ask which is bigger.

1.5.misconception: Any closed figure is a polygon (circles, curved sides). Surface it: sort card with a circle and a crossed figure.

1.6.misconception: The compass is only for circles, not for transferring lengths. Surface it: ask them to copy a segment without a ruler.

1.7.misconception: Every word can be defined. Surface it: dictionary chase for 'point' loops back on itself.

1.8.misconception: The converse of a true statement is true. Surface it: 'If it's a square, it's a rectangle' flipped.

1.9.misconception: A definition only has to work one way. Surface it: a 'kite' definition that also admits non-kites.

1.10.misconception: A proof is a list of true facts in any order. Surface it: give shuffled proof lines to reorder.

1.11.misconception: Indirect proof means proving the opposite is true. Surface it: ask what the contradiction contradicts.

1.12.misconception: Theorems and postulates are the same kind of thing. Surface it: sort statements by 'proved or assumed'.

2.1.misconception: Algebra steps don't need reasons. Surface it: solve an equation and name each property.

2.2.misconception: Distance can be negative. Surface it: points at -3 and 5 on a ruler, compute both ways.

2.3.note: Coordinate midpoint formula is beyond Jacobs 3.2 (Jacobs gives the number-line midpoint).
2.3.misconception: Midpoint is the difference of the endpoints over 2. Surface it: endpoints -2 and 8.

2.4.misconception: Read the wrong protractor scale. Surface it: an obtuse angle that reads 50 on the inner scale.

2.5.misconception: Bisecting means drawing any line through the middle by eye. Surface it: ask how they know it's exact.

2.6.misconception: Complementary angles must be adjacent. Surface it: two separate 30 and 60 angles; are they complementary?

2.7.misconception: Vertical means 'up and down'. Surface it: vertical angles drawn on a tilted X.

2.8.misconception: Perpendicular lines must be horizontal and vertical. Surface it: a tilted right angle.

2.9.misconception: Any arc width works for every step. Surface it: an arc smaller than half the segment.

2.10.misconception: Parallel construction just means 'draw it looking parallel'. Surface it: ask which angle pair the copy made equal.

2.11.misconception: Vertical angles are equal 'because they look it'. Surface it: require a theorem name per line.

2.12.misconception: Construction art is decoration, not math. Surface it: ask which construction each step of the design used.

3.1.note: Motion postulates (per Euclid, ANSWERS.md sec. 1): state here, as explicit postulates, that translations, rotations and reflections exist and preserve distance, angle measure, collinearity and betweenness (a reflection swaps half-planes). They are assumed, not proved, and every later congruence-by-motion argument (3.12, 4.3, 4.4) cites them.
3.1.misconception: The image and preimage are the same figure. Surface it: label A and A' on a slide.

3.2.misconception: A translation can turn the figure. Surface it: overlay a tilted image and ask if it's a translation.

3.3.misconception: Reflecting moves each point the same distance in one direction. Surface it: reflect over a slanted line.

3.4.misconception: Rotation is always about the origin. Surface it: rotate about a vertex of the figure.

3.5.misconception: Order of reflections doesn't matter. Surface it: reflect over two crossing lines in both orders.

3.6.misconception: Only one sequence of motions maps one figure to another. Surface it: collect different class sequences.

3.7.misconception: Dilations are rigid motions. Surface it: measure a side after a dilation.

3.9.misconception: A rectangle has diagonal lines of symmetry. Surface it: paper-fold a rectangle along a diagonal.

3.10.misconception: Point symmetry and line symmetry are the same. Surface it: the letter N and the letter A.

3.11.misconception: Any shape tessellates. Surface it: try regular pentagons.

3.12.note: Jacobs defines congruence by parts (4.2) and adds the isometry definition in 8.3, p. 312; this course leads with the isometry definition.
3.12.misconception: Congruent means 'same shape'. Surface it: two similar triangles of different size.

4.1.misconception: Order of letters in a congruence statement doesn't matter. Surface it: triangle ABC ≅ triangle FED vs triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF (use = only for lengths and measures).

4.2.misconception: Three matching parts of any kind is always enough. Surface it: SSA and AAA counterexample cards.

4.3.note: Jacobs takes SAS as Postulate 6 (p. 147); this course justifies it from rigid motions.
4.3.misconception: The included angle can be any angle. Surface it: mark a non-included angle and ask if SAS applies.

4.4.note: Jacobs takes ASA as Postulate 5 (p. 147); this course justifies it from rigid motions.
4.4.misconception: ASA and AAS are the same test. Surface it: mark which side is between the angles.

4.5.misconception: You can use what you're proving as a reason. Surface it: a proof that cites the goal.

4.6.misconception: CPCTC can be used before the triangles are proved congruent. Surface it: reorder a flawed proof.

4.7.misconception: Base angles are the angles at the bottom of the picture. Surface it: an isosceles triangle drawn upside down.

4.8.misconception: Equiangular and equilateral are separate facts to memorize. Surface it: ask which theorem gives each.

4.10.misconception: SSS is a postulate (it is a theorem in this course). Surface it: ask what SSS was proved from (SAS plus isosceles theorems, p. 164).

4.11.misconception: SSA works if the sides are long. Surface it: build two triangles from the same SSA data.

4.12.misconception: A construction is correct if it looks right. Surface it: name the congruence test behind each step.

4.13.misconception: Old constructions were already proved. Surface it: ask why the bisector construction from 2.5 works.

4.14.misconception: Every proof needs triangles congruent first. Surface it: a proof solvable by vertical angles alone.

5.1.misconception: Multiplying an inequality by a negative keeps the sign. Surface it: -2x < 6.

5.2.misconception: The exterior angle equals the sum of the remote interior angles here. Surface it: ask why only 'greater than' is allowed before the parallel postulate.

5.3.misconception: The longest side is next to the largest angle. Surface it: label a scalene triangle and ask for the side opposite.

5.4.misconception: Any three lengths make a triangle. Surface it: 2, 3, 6 straws.

5.5.note: Supplement: not in Jacobs. Kept and labeled Supplement on slide 1; proof route before the parallel postulate in Euclid ANSWERS.md sec. 3.
5.5.misconception: A wider angle always gives a longer side regardless of the other sides. Surface it: change a side length too.

5.6.misconception: Parallel tests assume the lines are parallel first. Surface it: ask what is given and what is proved.

5.8.misconception: The parallel postulate can be proved. Surface it: brief history of failed attempts (p. 225ff).

5.9.misconception: Same-side interior angles are equal. Surface it: measure them on a slanted transversal.

5.10.misconception: Angle sum 180 is true on any surface. Surface it: preview the sphere (16.1) as a teaser.

5.11.misconception: Exterior angle equals the adjacent interior angle. Surface it: label the remote interiors.

5.12.misconception: HL works for any triangle. Surface it: an obtuse triangle with matching side and 'hypotenuse'.

5.13.note: Jacobs treats slope in 11.6 (Thms 52 to 53, p. 463); this course moves it earlier.
5.13.misconception: Perpendicular slopes are negatives, not negative reciprocals. Surface it: slope 2 and slope -2 on a grid.

5.14.note: Writing line equations is beyond Jacobs.
5.14.misconception: Perpendicular line uses the same intercept. Surface it: substitute the point back in.

5.15.misconception: Two-column is the only valid proof form. Surface it: accept a flowchart and a paragraph version.

6.1.misconception: A square is not a rectangle. Surface it: quadrilateral family tree sort.

6.2.misconception: Parallelogram diagonals are equal. Surface it: measure on a slanted parallelogram.

6.3.misconception: Diagonals bisect the angles in every parallelogram. Surface it: measure on a non-rhombus.

6.4.misconception: One pair of parallel sides is enough. Surface it: a trapezoid.

6.5.misconception: A rhombus is a square. Surface it: a tilted rhombus with no right angles.

6.6.misconception: All trapezoids are isosceles. Surface it: a right trapezoid.

6.7.misconception: The midsegment is half of any side. Surface it: which side is it parallel to?

6.8.note: Coordinate proof of quadrilaterals is beyond Jacobs (needed for G.QP.2).
6.8.misconception: Showing one pair of slopes equal proves a parallelogram. Surface it: a trapezoid on a grid.

6.9.misconception: Exterior angle sum grows with sides. Surface it: walk the polygon on the floor.

6.10.misconception: Every equilateral polygon is regular. Surface it: a rhombus.

7.1.misconception: Area and perimeter grow together. Surface it: same perimeter, different areas with string.

7.2.misconception: Area units are linear units. Surface it: ask for the units on a 3 cm by 4 cm answer.

7.3.misconception: The height is always a side. Surface it: an obtuse triangle with an outside altitude.

7.4.misconception: Parallelogram area uses the slanted side. Surface it: shear a paper parallelogram into a rectangle.

7.5.misconception: Overlapping regions get counted once automatically. Surface it: an L-shape split two ways.

7.6.misconception: a squared plus b squared equals c squared for any triangle. Surface it: test an obtuse triangle.

7.7.misconception: The converse is the same theorem. Surface it: ask what is given in each direction.

7.9.note: Jacobs states the distance formula in 4.1 before proving Pythagoras; this course develops it after 9.5.
7.9.misconception: Distance formula is a new fact to memorize. Surface it: draw the right triangle on the grid first.

7.10.note: Perimeter and area on the coordinate plane extends Jacobs 4.1.
7.10.misconception: Count diagonal grid squares as 1 unit. Surface it: a diagonal side of length root 2.

7.11.misconception: One numeric example is a proof. Surface it: compare a specific example with variable coordinates.

7.12.misconception: Placement of axes doesn't matter for ease. Surface it: compare a corner-at-origin set-up with a random one.

8.1.misconception: Proportions can be cross-multiplied with any pairing. Surface it: set up a ratio with mismatched parts.

8.2.note: Jacobs uses dilations as motivation in 10.5; this course defines similarity by them.
8.2.misconception: A dilation adds a fixed amount to lengths. Surface it: scale factor 2 on a 3-4-5 triangle.

8.3.misconception: Dilations change angles. Surface it: measure angles before and after.

8.4.note: Jacobs defines similarity by correspondence (10.2); this course defines it by transformations.
8.4.misconception: Similar means 'roughly the same shape'. Surface it: two rectangles of different proportions.

8.5.misconception: Corresponding sides are found by position on the page. Surface it: a rotated similar polygon.

8.6.misconception: The side-splitter ratio uses the parallel segment. Surface it: label which pieces are proportional.

8.7.note: Partitioning a segment by coordinates is beyond Jacobs.
8.7.misconception: A 2:3 ratio means the point is 2/3 of the way. Surface it: ask for 2 parts of 5.

8.9.misconception: You need all three angles. Surface it: ask why two are enough (the angle sum).

8.10.misconception: SSA similarity works. Surface it: counterexample card.

8.11.note: Supplement: not a numbered Jacobs theorem (Euclid searched). Closest Jacobs item: 10.3, p. 397, Set II, ex. 48. Label Supplement on slide 1; needed for G.T.1f.
8.11.misconception: The bisector cuts the opposite side in half. Surface it: measure on a scalene triangle.

8.12.misconception: Area scales by k, not k squared. Surface it: tile a doubled square.

8.13.misconception: Every repeated pattern is self-similar. Surface it: a tiled floor vs. a Sierpinski triangle.

8.14.misconception: Shadow lengths aren't proportional at different times. Surface it: ask why both shadows must be measured at once.

9.1.misconception: The geometric mean is the average. Surface it: 4 and 9 give 6, not 6.5.

9.2.misconception: A second proof of a theorem is pointless. Surface it: ask what the similarity proof uses that the area proof did not.

9.3.misconception: The hypotenuse is 2 times the leg. Surface it: measure a 45-45-90 drawn on grid paper.

9.4.misconception: The root 3 goes on the hypotenuse. Surface it: ask which side is opposite the 60 degree angle.

9.5.misconception: Trig ratios depend on the triangle's size. Surface it: compare tan 30 in two sizes.

9.6.misconception: Opposite and adjacent are fixed sides. Surface it: switch the reference angle.

9.7.misconception: Sine can exceed 1. Surface it: ask which side is always the longest.

9.9.misconception: sin inverse means 1 over sin. Surface it: compare calculator outputs.

9.10.misconception: Slope and angle are proportional. Surface it: slope 1 is 45 degrees, slope 2 isn't 90.

9.11.misconception: Angle of depression is measured from the vertical. Surface it: draw the horizontal line first.

9.12.misconception: Always reach for Pythagoras first. Surface it: problems where only one angle and one side are known.

9.13.misconception: The Law of Sines always gives one triangle. Surface it: the ambiguous case (Euclid to confirm Jacobs' coverage).

10.1.misconception: A chord and a radius are the same. Surface it: label card sort.

10.2.misconception: Any line through a chord's midpoint passes through the center. Surface it: it must also be perpendicular.

10.3.misconception: A tangent can touch at two points. Surface it: drag a line across a circle.

10.4.misconception: Arc measure is arc length. Surface it: same arc degrees on two circles.

10.5.misconception: An inscribed angle equals its arc. Surface it: measure both.

10.6.misconception: Any quadrilateral can be inscribed in a circle. Surface it: try a non-isosceles trapezoid.

10.7.note: Present as a corollary of earlier circle-angle theorems (Euclid ANSWERS.md): tangents PA, PB give right angles OAP and OBP (12.2), the quadrilateral angle sum (Ch 7) gives angle APB + angle AOB = 180, so angle APB = 180 minus the minor arc AB.
10.7.misconception: A circumscribed angle equals the arc. Surface it: measure.

10.9.misconception: Every secant angle is half the sum of arcs. Surface it: vertex inside vs. outside.

10.10.misconception: Segment products use whole lengths for chords. Surface it: label the pieces.

10.11.misconception: The circumcenter is always inside. Surface it: an obtuse triangle.

10.12.misconception: Incenter and circumcenter are the same point. Surface it: construct both on one triangle.

10.13.misconception: Medians and altitudes are the same segment. Surface it: a scalene triangle.

10.14.misconception: Surprising coincidences are luck. Surface it: drag the triangle and watch Napoleon's triangle stay equilateral.

11.1.misconception: Perimeter of a regular polygon needs every side measured. Surface it: give one side and n.

11.2.misconception: The apothem is the radius. Surface it: label both on a hexagon.

11.3.misconception: Pi equals 22/7 or 3.14 exactly. Surface it: compare the polygon perimeters as n grows.

11.4.misconception: C = pi r. Surface it: measure a can with string.

11.5.misconception: Doubling r doubles area. Surface it: tile two circles.

11.6.misconception: Arc length equals arc degrees. Surface it: same 60 degree arc on two radii.

11.7.misconception: Segment area equals sector area. Surface it: subtract the triangle visibly.

11.8.note: Core, not enrichment: Jacobs 14.6, p. 608, heading The Radian, Set I ex. 26 to 30 (PDF p. 628). Derive angle = s/r, 180 degrees = pi radians.
11.8.misconception: Radians are a different kind of angle. Surface it: lay radius-length string along the arc.

12.1.misconception: Two lines that don't meet are parallel. Surface it: skew lines with two pencils.

12.2.note: Nets and cross sections extend Jacobs 15.2 to 15.3.
12.2.misconception: A cube's cross section is always a square. Surface it: the hexagon slice.

12.3.misconception: Slanted stacks have more volume. Surface it: shear a stack of coins.

12.4.misconception: Volume of a cylinder uses the diameter. Surface it: units check.

12.5.misconception: A pyramid is half a prism. Surface it: pour rice from pyramid into prism.

12.6.misconception: Sphere volume is 4 pi r squared. Surface it: units check (cubic vs. square).

12.8.misconception: Surface area and volume are interchangeable. Surface it: units on each.

12.9.note: Composite solids with algebraic expressions (G.TS.4) are beyond Jacobs exercises; Euclid to confirm.
12.9.misconception: Shared faces count toward surface area. Surface it: two stacked cubes.

12.10.misconception: Volume scales by k squared. Surface it: build a doubled cube from unit cubes.

12.11.misconception: There are infinitely many regular polyhedra. Surface it: try to build one from hexagons.

12.14.misconception: Straight lines on a sphere are like latitude lines. Surface it: string on a ball between two cities.
